blocks.text:
Meningococcal vaccination is administered to help the body develop immunity against meningococcal meningitis, an infection of the protective membranes surrounding the brain and spinal cord caused by the bacterium Neisseria meningitidis.

This vaccine is recommended for individuals traveling to regions where meningococcal disease is endemic. For those performing Hajj or Umrah pilgrimages, meningococcal vaccination is mandatory and is one of the requirements for obtaining a visa from the Embassy of the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia.

The protection provided by the vaccine is valid for two years.
Meningococcal Vaccination Before Umrah or Hajj

In preparation for Umrah or Hajj, the Meningococcal ACW135Y vaccine is available at Port Health Offices (Kantor Kesehatan Pelabuhan/KKP) throughout Indonesia.

After receiving the vaccination, pilgrims are issued an International Certificate of Vaccination (ICV), which is required when applying for a visa.

The vaccine administered is Menveo ACW135Y Meningococcal Vaccine, which has been approved by the Indonesian Food and Drug Authority (Badan POM) and has been certified Halal by the Indonesian Ulema Council (Majelis Ulama Indonesia/MUI).

Meningococcal vaccination is a mandatory requirement for all Hajj and Umrah pilgrims in accordance with the regulations established by the Government of Saudi Arabia. To ensure optimal protection, the vaccine should be administered at least two weeks before departure.

The purpose of vaccination is to protect pilgrims against meningococcal meningitis for up to three years.
Preventing Transmission

In addition to protecting individual pilgrims, vaccination also helps prevent the spread of meningococcal disease among pilgrims from around the world and reduces the risk of transmitting the infection to family members after returning home.

Meningococcal meningitis is transmitted through respiratory droplets and secretions from the nose and throat when an infected person coughs or sneezes. The disease attacks the protective membranes surrounding the brain and spinal cord (meninges) and can lead to permanent disability or even death if left untreated.
Why Are Women Asked About Their Last Menstrual Period?

Women are routinely asked about the first day of their last menstrual period before receiving the meningococcal vaccine to determine whether there is a possibility of pregnancy.

If pregnancy cannot be ruled out, an hCG (Human Chorionic Gonadotropin) test may be performed before vaccination. This examination is available in the laboratory.

Meningococcal vaccination is not recommended during pregnancy, as it may pose risks to the developing fetus.
Who Should Not Receive the Vaccine?
Besides pregnant women, this vaccine is generally not recommended for:

items: Infants younger than 2 months of age.
Individuals who have contraindications as determined by their healthcare provider.

blocks.text:
For adults and children over 5 years of age, a single dose provides protection against meningococcal disease for approximately 5 years.

For children under 5 years of age, protection generally lasts 2 to 3 years. Infants and children aged 2 months to 3 years require a second dose three months after the first vaccination.
What Are the Possible Side Effects?

Serious side effects following meningococcal vaccination are very rare.

Approximately 10% of vaccinated individuals may experience pain or redness at the injection site, which usually resolves within 1 to 2 days. Children may occasionally develop a mild fever after vaccination.
Meningococcal Vaccination During Pregnancy

If you are pregnant, it is important to be cautious when considering any vaccination. Many cases of viral and bacterial meningitis can be prevented through immunization. If you are unsure whether your vaccinations are up to date, consult your doctor.

Available vaccines include:

items: MMR Vaccine (Measles, Mumps, and Rubella): The first dose is recommended at 12 months of age, followed by a booster between 5 and 7 years of age.
Pneumococcal Conjugate Vaccine (PCV): For infants under one year of age, the vaccine is administered every two months. For children over two years of age, a single dose is generally sufficient.
DTaP/IPV/Hib Vaccine: Provides protection against Haemophilus influenzae type b (Hib), diphtheria, pertussis (whooping cough), tetanus, and poliovirus.

blocks.text:
Although the meningococcal vaccine is not included in Indonesia's routine childhood immunization schedule, it is available in Indonesia.

Please consult your doctor if you wish to receive any of these vaccines.
Meningococcal Vaccination for Travel

The bacterium Neisseria meningitidis (meningococcus) is relatively uncommon in Indonesia. As a result, many Indonesians do not have natural immunity against this bacterium.

Vaccination is strongly recommended for individuals traveling to areas where meningococcal disease is more prevalent, particularly Saudi Arabia and several countries in Africa.

Individuals planning to perform Umrah are required to receive the meningococcal vaccine before departure to reduce the risk of contracting meningococcal disease.
Traveling to High-Risk Areas
Vaccination against Meningococcal Groups A, C, Y, and W135 is strongly recommended for anyone traveling to high-risk regions, especially if you plan to:

items: Stay with local residents in densely populated areas while performing Hajj or Umrah in Saudi Arabia.
Work in Hajj-related activities, including seasonal employment or overseas work assignments in Saudi Arabia.
Stay for more than one month as a long-term traveler or visitor.

blocks.text: Meningococcal Vaccination for Infants

For infants between 2 months and 2 years of age, the initial vaccine dose should be followed by a second dose three months later.

The meningococcal vaccine is not recommended for infants younger than 2 months.

For children under 5 years of age, the vaccine provides protection for approximately 2 to 3 years. For adults and children 5 years of age and older, a single dose provides protection for approximately 5 years.

Protection against Meningococcal Groups A, C, Y, and W135 requires the Meningococcal ACYW135 vaccine.
Side Effects of the Meningococcal Vaccine

The vaccine should ideally be administered 2 to 4 weeks before travel.

Approximately 1 in 10 people receiving the Meningococcal ACWY vaccine may experience mild pain, redness, or a rash at the injection site. These side effects usually resolve within 1 to 2 days.

Serious adverse reactions are extremely rare. Mild fever may occur after vaccination and is more commonly observed in children than in adults.

Meningococcal disease is caused by the bacterium Neisseria meningitidis. It is transmitted from person to person through respiratory droplets and saliva, with an incubation period of approximately 3 to 4 days.

Meningococcal disease should not be underestimated, as it can lead to severe complications and even death.

Another infectious disease that pilgrims should be aware of while in the Holy Land is influenza. Unlike the common cold, influenza presents with more severe symptoms and is caused exclusively by the influenza virus.

The influenza viruses that most commonly infect humans are Influenza A and Influenza B. Examples of Influenza A strains include H1N1 and H3N2, while Influenza B strains include Victoria and Yamagata.

Like meningococcal disease, influenza can also be life-threatening. According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), seasonal influenza causes an estimated 291,000 to 646,000 deaths worldwide each year.

According to Dr. Iris Rengganis, Sp.PD, an Allergy and Immunology Specialist from the Department of Internal Medicine, Faculty of Medicine, Universitas Indonesia – Cipto Mangunkusumo Hospital (FKUI-RSCM), travelers should prepare themselves before visiting another country by understanding the risk of infectious diseases that may be prevalent at their destination.

Every country has its own endemic diseases. Travelers should familiarize themselves with the health risks of the country they plan to visit. For example, the risk of contracting meningococcal disease is high in Saudi Arabia, while typhoid fever and hepatitis are more common in Indonesia. (Jakarta, February 14, 2013)
blocks.author: Dr. Iris Rengganis, Sp.PD
blocks.role: Allergy and Immunology Specialist, Department of Internal Medicine, Faculty of Medicine, Universitas Indonesia – Cipto Mangunkusumo Hospital (FKUI-RSCM)

blocks.text:
Vaccination is considered one of the most important primary preventive measures for international travelers.

"Several countries require visitors to receive certain vaccinations before entering their territory," she explained.

Diseases that can be prevented through vaccination include meningococcal disease, influenza, typhoid fever, yellow fever, tetanus, and hepatitis.

When receiving vaccinations, several important factors should be considered. Vaccines should be potent, capable of stimulating the immune system to produce adequate antibodies, safe for recipients, and compliant with international standards established by the World Health Organization (WHO).

Dr. Iris also recommends receiving vaccinations 2 weeks to 1 month before travel to allow sufficient time for protective antibodies to develop.

While at the destination, travelers are advised to maintain healthy habits, such as washing their hands before eating and after using public restrooms, maintaining good physical health through a balanced diet and regular exercise, choosing food appropriate to their dietary habits, and bringing suitable clothing for the climate of the destination country.
Benefits of Meningococcal Vaccination

Vaccines contain antigens, substances that stimulate the body's immune system to produce protective antibodies.

These antibodies help defend the body by destroying bacteria that invade the immune system.

Meningococcal vaccination has an effectiveness rate of approximately 85% to 90% in preventing meningococcal disease.

However, because the vaccine does not protect against every strain of bacteria that can cause meningitis, vaccinated individuals may still develop meningitis caused by strains not covered by the vaccine.

Even so, receiving the meningococcal vaccine significantly reduces the risk of contracting meningococcal disease and its potentially serious complications.
